name: The Kolmogorov Zero-One Law
statement: Any tail event of a sequence of independent random variables has probability either exactly zero or exactly one.
statementAccent: probability either exactly zero or exactly one
meaning: A tail event is one whose occurrence does not depend on the outcome of any finite subset of the independent random variables; it is unaffected by changing finitely many of them. The law states such an event can only have probability 0 or 1, never an intermediate value. It thus splits tail events into those that almost surely happen and those that almost surely do not.
mechanism: The tail sigma-algebra is the intersection of the sigma-algebras generated by the variables from index n onward. By independence, any tail event is independent of each finite-dimensional sub-algebra and hence independent of the sigma-algebra they generate, which contains the tail event itself. An event independent of itself has probability equal to its square, forcing the probability to be 0 or 1.

examples.text: Whether a sum of independent random variables converges is a tail event, so it converges either almost surely or almost never.
For independent coin tosses, the event that a run of 100 consecutive heads occurs infinitely often has probability 0 or 1.
The existence of an infinite connected cluster in independent percolation is a tail-type event whose probability is 0 or 1.

whyItMatters: The law is a foundational result in probability theory that underpins limit theorems, ergodic arguments, and the study of almost-sure behavior of infinite random sequences. It shows that many asymptotic properties are deterministic in probability even when individual outcomes are random.
limits: It requires the random variables to be independent, and it identifies only that the probability is 0 or 1 without telling which; determining the actual value can be difficult. It applies to tail events specifically, not to events that depend materially on finitely many variables.
misreadings: It does not say every event has probability 0 or 1, only tail events of independent variables, and it does not by itself reveal whether the answer is 0 or 1.
origin: Andrey Kolmogorov, Russian mathematician (1903–1987), 1933, in Grundbegriffe der Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung.

sources.text: Wikipedia's "Kolmogorov's zero-one law" article, stating that a tail event of independent sigma-algebras has probability 0 or 1 and the difficulty of deciding which — supports the statement and mechanism.
Wikipedia's "Andrey Kolmogorov" article, confirming his dates and his 1933 axiomatic foundations of probability containing the zero-one law — supports the attribution.
